english.html: certain news of the husband's death <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>. Of which the chaste Penelope once engraved a holy and eternally memorable example upon the tablets of posterity. For during the absence of Ulysses her spouse (which was, however, of twenty years), she could never be overcome by the continual entreaties of her relatives, nor persuaded, by the urgent solicitations of countless young men (who sought to have her to wife), to remarry.

notes.citation: Digest 24.2.6 (De divortiis et repudiis, l. Uxores); Code 5.17.7 (De repudiis, l. Uxor) with the authentica Hodie (from Nov. 117 c. 11); Novel 22 (De nuptiis, coll. 4), § Sed etiam; Decretals, X 4.1 (De sponsalibus et matrimoniis), c. In praesentia (cf. X 4.1.19)
notes.original: L. vxores. D. de diuor. L. vxor. & autẽtique hodie. C. de repud. Paragr. ſed etiam. de nup. aux nouuelles de Iuſtinien ſous la iiij. collation c. in præſentia. de ſponſal.
notes.gloss: Julian: the wives of men in enemy hands keep the status of married women, since they cannot rashly marry another; the Code law and the authentica on the soldier's wife who has no news; the decretal forbidding remarriage without certain proof of the husband's death.

english.html: Penelope was able to live untouched through twice ten years, a woman worthy of so many suitors (Penelope poterat, bis denos salva per annos, / vivere, tam multis foemina digna procis). h

notes.original: Properce au liure ij. de ſes elegies.

english.html: And because, besides the excellent and native beauty with which nature had happily enriched her, she was further commended by I know not what ray of virtue, gentleness and simplicity, which made her lovable and admirable in the eyes of all, she was violently pressed, and solicited almost by force, by her suitors: to repulse whom graciously, she obtained from them a delay until she should have finished weaving the little piece of cloth that she had in hand (which they granted her), hoping to see the cloth soon woven: but she, having her heart always with her Ulysses, to cheat these gentle lovers of their foolish hope, unravelled by night what she had woven by day: and thus kept them waiting and deceived them until the return of her consort <sup class="mk" data-key="i">i</sup>. Wherefore one must not be so impious as to think that, if the wife had prostituted herself during the husband's absence (and he for that reason has driven her out), and she asked to be reinstated in her marriage, the adultery would not justly be objected against her <sup class="mk" data-key="k">k</sup>: unless the husband had lent a hand to his wife's misconduct, and to that end had deliberately absented himself <sup class="mk" data-key="l">l</sup>. For although that does not excuse the wife, who for anything in the world ought not to be so liberal with her honour, which she ought to hold a thousand times dearer than life <sup class="mk" data-key="m">m</sup>: nevertheless it charges the husband, and makes him so far culpable that he would without difficulty be punished as his wife's pander; so far is it from his being able to object or reproach such a fault against her in judgment <sup class="mk" data-key="n">n</sup>.
